title: Course overview
focus: Learn language concepts by defining a small language and implementing its interpreter. OCaml is the implementation tool; the interpreted language is a separate object of study.
points: The course connects inductive definitions, functional programming, interpreters, and static analysis.
Syntax describes programs; semantics describes their meaning; an implementation must preserve that meaning.
Use the official course page for current logistics. This sheet concentrates on the technical learning path.
formula: program → syntax tree → interpreter → value; program → type checker → type or rejection
steps: Read its syntax and semantic rules
Trace a small example before implementing
example: A course expression such as proc x (x + 1) becomes an AST value; the OCaml evaluator then interprets that value. Writing an OCaml function and interpreting a function in the toy language are different tasks.
homework: All four assignments follow this progression.
check: What is the difference between the language of the interpreter and the language it interprets?
answer: The interpreter is written in OCaml. Its input represents a program in the specified course language.

title: Inductive definitions I
focus: Define an infinite set using finite base and construction rules, with no extra elements.
points: Top-down, bottom-up, and inference-rule presentations describe the same generated set when their rules agree.
An axiom starts a derivation; a rule builds a larger derivation from premises.
Membership requires a finite derivation. Showing a property is preserved only proves one direction of set equality.
formula: 0 ∈ S; n ∈ S ⇒ n + 3 ∈ S; therefore S = {3k | k ≥ 0}
steps: Prove both inclusions for a claimed set equality
example: To derive 6 ∈ S, derive 0 first, then 3, then 6. To prove S contains exactly the nonnegative multiples of 3, prove generated elements are multiples and every such multiple can be generated.
homework: HW1 P11: ZERO and SUCC are the base and constructor of Peano naturals.
check: Does closure under adding 3 alone exclude 1 from S?
answer: No. The least-set requirement excludes elements not generated from the bases.

title: Inductive definitions II
focus: The shape of a datatype determines the cases of its recursive functions and structural proofs.
points: Lists and trees need distinct rules for each constructor.
Expression grammar describes syntax; an evaluator separately assigns meanings.
A structural induction hypothesis applies to the immediate recursive components, not an arbitrary larger object.
formula: P(base); P(a) ∧ P(b) ⇒ P(Node(a,b)); hence P(t) for every generated tree t
steps: Assume the property for each recursive child
Combine the child facts in the constructor case
example: For a full binary tree with Leaf and Fork(left,right), prove leaves = forks + 1: Leaf gives 1 = 0 + 1; Fork combines the two hypotheses and adds one fork.
homework: HW1 P9–P13: match the exact tree, natural-number, formula, or expression constructors.
check: Can the same tree cases be copied from mem.ml to mirror.ml?
answer: No. The official files use different tree datatypes; inspect each constructor list.

title: Basics of OCaml
focus: Read OCaml as expressions built from bindings, functions, patterns, and typed values.
points: let binds a value; let ... in limits the binding to a body. Ordinary bindings are not assignments.
Function application uses spaces; curried functions return functions when partially applied.
Lists are homogeneous; tuples may mix types. Pattern matching decomposes constructors.
Exceptions and modules are language tools, but the homework may restrict their use: HW2 forbids modules.
formula: fun x -> e : α -> β when x : α and e : β; h :: t : α list when h : α and t : α list
steps: Determine the input and output types
Check every branch returns a compatible type
example: let add x y = x + y defines int -> int -> int. add 2 returns an int -> int function; add 2 3 evaluates to 5.
homework: All HW1 signatures; HW2–HW4 AST pattern matches.
check: Why is [1; true] rejected while (1, true) is allowed?
answer: List elements share one type; tuple positions have independently specified types.

title: Recursion and higher-order programming
focus: Solve a smaller instance, then combine its result; abstract repeated traversal with functions.
points: A recursive call must move toward a base case.
Tail recursion leaves no pending computation after the recursive call; an accumulator needs an invariant.
map transforms elements, filter selects them, and folds combine them.
Fold direction changes association and argument order, especially for subtraction and list construction.
formula: fold_right f [a;b] z = f a (f b z); fold_left f z [a;b] = f (f z a) b
homework: HW1 P2–P8 and P9–P15; textbook §2.4 especially Problems 8–10.
check: Is 1 + length tail a tail call?
answer: No. Addition remains after length returns.

title: Expressions and environments
focus: Translate each evaluation rule into a matching AST case and keep the environment explicit.
points: Syntax, semantic domains, and evaluation rules serve different roles.
The environment maps identifiers to runtime values; nearest bindings shadow older ones.
A let initializer uses the old environment; only its body uses the extension.
A conditional evaluates its guard and one selected branch.
formula: ρ ⊢ e1 ⇒ v1; ρ[x ↦ v1] ⊢ e2 ⇒ v2; therefore ρ ⊢ let x = e1 in e2 ⇒ v2
example: let x = 2 in let x = x + 1 in x evaluates to 3. The inner initializer sees the outer x; the final x sees the inner binding.
homework: HW2: constants, arithmetic, variables, IF, and LET. HW1 P12 provides a smaller evaluator.
check: Should both branches of IF be evaluated?
answer: No. Doing so can introduce errors or effects that the language does not require.

title: Procedures and recursive closures
focus: A lexical procedure carries the environment where it was defined; a call extends that saved environment.
points: A closure contains parameter, body, and definition environment.
Evaluate the callee and argument in the caller environment, but run the body in the captured environment.
Dynamic scope instead uses the caller environment; it is a different semantics.
Recursive and mutually recursive closures must restore the appropriate function bindings at invocation.
formula: closure = (x, body, ρdef); call body in ρdef[x ↦ varg] (plus recursive bindings when required)
example: let x = 10 in let f = proc y (x + y) in let x = 100 in f 3 returns 13 under lexical scope and 103 under dynamic scope.
homework: HW2 PROC, CALL, LETREC, LETMREC; textbook Chapter 4 scope exercises and Chapter 5 Fun implementation.
check: Which environment supplies free x in a lexical closure body?
answer: The definition environment saved in the closure, extended by the call's bindings.

title: Lexical addresses and nameless programs
focus: Resolve a variable to its binder statically and replace names with positions.
points: A declaration introduces a binder; a reference is a use of a name.
Search outward from the nearest binder, so shadowing changes the address.
Translation uses a name context; evaluation uses a value environment with the same layout.
An unbound name cannot be assigned a valid lexical address.
formula: index(x, [x0; x1; ...]) = least i such that xi = x; #0 denotes the nearest binder
steps: Push a binder on entering its scope
Replace each use with its position
Evaluate positions in the matching value list
example: proc x (proc y (x - y)) becomes proc (proc (#1 - #0)). At the subtraction, y is nearest and x is one level farther out.
homework: Conceptual support for HW1 P15 binding checks and HW2 lexical environments; no separate nameless-language homework is specified.
check: In let x = e1 in e2, does x enter the context for e1?
answer: Not for an ordinary nonrecursive let. Extend the context only for e2.

title: State and parameter passing
focus: Separate the binding map from mutable memory and carry the updated store through every evaluation step.
points: Explicit references make locations values; implicit references make variables denote locations.
Allocation chooses a fresh location; assignment updates an existing location.
Call by value uses a fresh parameter cell; call by reference aliases a caller cell.
Lazy evaluation delays argument computation; it is distinct from passing a location.
formula: ρ : Var → Loc, M : Loc → Value; variable value = M(ρ(x)); eval returns (v, M′)
steps: Update or read the selected cell
example: If a is stored at L0 with value 3, passing a by reference to a procedure that assigns 4 changes L0. Passing by value creates a different parameter cell and leaves a at 3.
homework: HW3 variables, assignment, SEQ, CALLV, CALLR, and loops; textbook Chapter 6.
check: Can the right operand start with the original memory?
answer: No. It must receive the memory produced by the left operand when the specified order is left to right.

title: Records, pointers, and garbage collection
focus: Follow locations through structured values and distinguish unreachable memory from memory that merely looks unused.
points: A record maps field names to locations, allowing field updates and shared records.
First-class pointers let locations themselves be stored and passed.
Manual freeing can create dangling references; automatic collection retains reachable cells.
Reachability is a conservative approximation to future use. Runtime roots may include pending computation as well as environments.
formula: R0 = roots; R(i+1) = Ri ∪ successors(Ri); stop at a fixed point and retain M restricted to R
steps: Repeat until no new location appears
example: Two variables can point to the same record field cell. Updating the field through one alias is visible through the other. A visited set prevents a cyclic pointer graph from making traversal loop forever.
homework: HW3 RECORD, FIELD, ASSIGNF; the GC exercises belong to textbook Chapter 7, not the HW3 required AST.
check: Does reachable imply the cell will definitely be read again?
answer: No. Keeping all reachable cells is safe but can retain cells that are never used again.

title: Exceptions and continuations
focus: Make pending computation explicit so a raised exception can discard frames up to the nearest handler.
points: A continuation represents the computation that remains after the current expression.
Ordinary evaluation applies a continuation to a value.
try installs a handler with its environment; raise evaluates a payload then searches outward.
The handler runs outside the handled continuation segment; discarded arithmetic does not resume.
formula: try (1 + raise 5) catch x x ⇒ 5; the waiting addition frame is discarded
steps: Install a handler frame for try
Discard frames to the nearest handler
Run the handler in its saved environment
example: try (5 + raise 9) catch x (x + 2) returns 11, not 16. An unhandled raise has no matching handler and cannot produce an ordinary result.
homework: An extension of the HW2 interpreter model; exceptions are not required constructors in that starter. Use the companion exception trace for practice.
check: Does the handler resume the abandoned addition?
answer: No. The continuation frames above the handler have been removed.

title: Classes and objects
focus: An object combines mutable field locations with a class identity used for method lookup.
points: Build the class environment before evaluating the main expression.
Inherited field locations persist in each object; field shadowing requires distinct identities.
A normal message send dispatches from the receiver's runtime class.
super begins lookup at the parent of the method's host class while retaining the same receiver.
formula: object = (runtime class, field environment); method lookup walks the class chain
steps: Run method with fields parameters and self
example: If a child overrides m, self.m() can choose the override. A super.m() in a method starts from the host class's parent and does not allocate a new parent object.
homework: Extends HW3 environments and memory. No class-language implementation is specified in HW1–HW4.
check: Is self always an object of the method's declaring class?
answer: No. An inherited method may run with a receiver whose runtime class is a subclass.

title: Why static types?
focus: Use a computable static approximation to prevent a specified class of runtime type errors.
points: Perfect automatic prediction of arbitrary program behavior is undecidable; useful restricted analyses remain possible.
Sound acceptance guarantees the intended safety property, under the language's assumptions.
A sound type system may reject some programs that would execute safely.
Type safety does not imply termination or the absence of every possible software bug.
formula: accepted ⇒ no specified runtime type error; safe ⇏ necessarily accepted
steps: Name the runtime errors being excluded
example: A checker that requires both IF branches to have one type rejects if true then 1 else false even though this particular execution selects the integer branch.
homework: HW4: understand what successful typeof promises and why an untypable expression raises TypeError.
check: Does a sound type checker prove a program terminates?
answer: No. A well-typed recursive program may diverge.

title: Designing typing rules
focus: Build typing derivations using a type environment instead of executing the program.
points: Types are inductively built from base and function types.
The context Γ maps variables to types, not runtime values.
A procedure extends Γ with its parameter type; application matches argument and domain.
The declarative rules may permit multiple types for one expression.
formula: Γ,x:α ⊢ e:β ⇒ Γ ⊢ proc x e:α→β; Γ ⊢ f:α→β and Γ ⊢ a:α ⇒ Γ ⊢ f a:β
steps: Choose the rule for the outer constructor
example: proc x (if x then 11 else 22) has bool → int: the guard forces x to bool and both branches have int.
homework: HW4: derive one rule per AST constructor before implementing inference.
check: Why cannot Γ simply contain runtime values?
answer: Typing runs before execution and tracks types; values belong to the runtime environment.

title: Manual type annotations
focus: Explicit procedure annotations make syntax-directed checking possible without guessing parameter types.
points: A recursive type checker follows the AST and compares inferred child types.
Annotated parameters supply information missing from an unannotated procedure.
Recursive functions need an assumed signature while checking their own bodies.
The body must agree with the declared result; an annotation is a claim to verify.
formula: check(proc (x:α) e, Γ) = α → check(e, Γ[x ↦ α])
example: proc (x:int) (x + 1) checks as int → int. proc (x:bool) (x + 1) is rejected because arithmetic requires int.
homework: Preparation for HW4, whose unannotated expressions require fresh unknowns and constraints instead of asking the user for annotations.
check: Can the checker trust an annotation without checking the body?
answer: No. Otherwise inconsistent annotations could admit unsafe operations.

title: Type inference I: the idea
focus: Infer unknown types from how expressions are used, by turning typing rules into equations.
points: Use fresh type variables for unknown parameter and expression types.
Arithmetic forces int; a guard forces bool; branch results must agree.
A call forces the callee type to argument type → result type.
Soundness/completeness of inference relative to a type system is different from completeness for all runtime-safe programs.
formula: f a : β contributes type(f) = type(a) → β
steps: Apply the solution to the result type
example: proc f (proc x (f (x + 1))) forces x:int and f:int→β, giving (int→β)→int→β.
homework: HW4: plan fresh_tyvar use and expected constraints for each constructor.
check: Is a type variable a variable in the interpreted program?
answer: No. It is an unknown in the checker's description of types.

title: Type inference II: constraint generation
focus: Define V(Γ,e,t) to generate the equalities required for expression e to have target type t.
points: The generator is recursive on syntax and produces constraints rather than runtime values.
Allocate fresh variables locally for unknown child types.
Binder occurrences share the type recorded in Γ; do not invent a new type for every use of the same monomorphic variable.
Generation can succeed even when the resulting equations are inconsistent.
formula: V(Γ, f a, t) = V(Γ,f,α→t) ∪ V(Γ,a,α), with fresh α
steps: Receive context expression and target type
Generate child constraints in proper contexts
example: For (proc x x) 1 with target β, generate the procedure's parameter/result equality and int for the argument. Solving forces β=int.
homework: HW4: implement a constraint generator before unification; add the starter's list and recursive-function cases.
check: Should two independent procedure parameters receive the same fresh type variable?
answer: No. They become equal only if a constraint requires it.

title: Type inference III: unification
focus: Solve type equations by substitution, decomposition, mismatch rejection, and the occurs check.
points: Normalize both sides using the current substitution before comparing.
Function equality decomposes into domain and codomain equality; lists decompose by element type.
Bind a variable only if it does not occur inside its proposed replacement.
Apply the final substitution to the provisional result type, not just to the remaining constraints.
formula: unify(α, int) gives [α↦int]; unify(α, α→β) fails; S(t1→t2)=S(t1)→S(t2)
steps: Compose and propagate a new binding
example: α=β→β and β=int give α=int→int. For proc f (f f), the equation α=α→β fails the occurs check under finite simple types.
homework: HW4: substitution, unification, occurs check, final result normalization, and TypeError tests.
check: Why is α=α harmless but α=α→β rejected?
answer: The first is identity. The second requires an infinite type in this finite-type system.

title: Let-polymorphism
focus: Generalize independent type variables at let bindings and instantiate them freshly at each use.
points: A scheme ∀α.t represents a family of instances, not a single shared unknown.
Never generalize variables constrained by the environment.
Procedure parameters remain monomorphic in the presented let-polymorphic system.
The pure-language rule cannot be transferred blindly to mutable references; practical OCaml uses a value restriction.
formula: Gen(Γ,t)=∀(FTV(t)−FTV(Γ)).t; Inst(∀α.t)=t[α↦fresh β]
steps: Infer and solve the let initializer
Apply substitutions to type and context
Generalize variables absent from the context
Bind the identifier to its generalized scheme
example: let id = proc x x in if id true then id 11 else id 22 uses independent bool→bool and int→int instances. A monomorphic id would force bool=int and fail.
homework: HW4 handout does not settle every polymorphism policy. Implement the required policy explicitly; this lecture explains the extension rather than silently changing the assignment contract.
check: Can a type variable free in Γ be quantified at this let?
answer: No. It represents a dependency on the surrounding context.

title: Typed objects and subtyping
focus: Check class programs using safe substitutability, with contravariant method inputs and covariant outputs.
points: Class inheritance establishes the nominal subtype relation in this lecture language.
Subsumption permits an expression of a subtype where a supertype is required.
Build class signatures and validate overrides before checking method bodies and the main expression.
The receiver's static type controls available members; runtime dispatch still selects the implementation.
steps: Build inherited field and method signatures
Check each method body in its context
Use subtyping at permitted compatibility checks
example: If ColorPoint <: Point, a replacement for Point→Point may accept every Point and return ColorPoint. Restricting its input to ColorPoint is unsafe for callers supplying an ordinary Point.
homework: An extension beyond HW4's simple type checker; do not replace equality unification with subtyping in HW4 without a specification change.
check: May an override demand a narrower argument type?
answer: Not under the lecture's substitutability rule: old callers must still be accepted.

title: Lambda calculus
focus: Understand functions and application as a small core, then make binding and reduction strategy precise.
points: Terms consist only of variables, abstraction, and application.
Beta reduction substitutes an argument without capturing its free variables; alpha-renaming may be necessary.
Normal order reduces leftmost outermost redexes and may reduce under lambdas; call by name does not reduce under lambdas.
Church encodings represent booleans and natural numbers as functions; fixed points express recursion, with evaluation-strategy caveats.
formula: (λx.e) a →β e[x:=a], using capture-avoiding substitution
steps: Choose a redex under the chosen strategy
Rename binders if capture is possible
Repeat or identify a normal form
example: (λx.λy.x) y must become λz.y after renaming the inner y. The incorrect λy.y captures the formerly free argument variable.
homework: HW2's fixed-point discussion and textbook Chapter 9 encoding tasks; this is not OCaml surface syntax.
check: Does the usual Y combinator directly terminate under eager call by value?
answer: No. Its self-application unfolds eagerly; use a strategy-appropriate delayed fixed-point construction.
